OA.3 The rich economies with the design given

Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S., France and the UK, and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time, its pension design, its demography and the characteristics that set France apart; appendix F gives the data and the household heterogeneity behind the calibration. This chapter holds every table behind section 6’s figure, the counterfactuals under CRRA preferences and the same counterfactuals with the UK as host, each under both calibrations of the taste for leisure, and the calibrations at every intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) of the model’s grid.

OA.3.1 Calibration

The first table prints the country parameters, with those the three countries share in a lower panel; the others print, by income group, the population shares, the taste for leisure, the productivities and the propensities to vote. France is grouped at the U.S. income percentiles and, for the UK as host, at the UK’s. The UK is also regrouped at the U.S. percentiles for one row of the paper’s cross-country test in section 7; that regrouping is a linear fit of the UK’s own group means against their cumulative population shares, not a recount of the survey.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

Table 3 of the paper: the three calibrations at an IES of one. France has the lowest population growth and the narrowest productivity spread of the three and the U.S. the highest population growth, while the political weight of the old is close in the U.S. and France and lower in the UK.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration only \(X\), whose level is the unit of hours, and the productivity spread change; \(\theta\), \(\omega\), the demography and the shared parameters are those of the common \(X\). The spread widens in all three countries, the UK’s now slightly above the U.S. one, and France’s stays the narrowest.

Table 6 of the paper: the U.S. households in three income groups, the first two cut so that their mean incomes are half the mean and the mean. Productivity and the propensity to vote both rise with income, and the low group holds most households.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the taste for leisure differs across the groups, identified from relative hours, and rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart than under the common \(X\); the population shares and the propensities to vote are data and do not change.

Table 7 of the paper: France’s households grouped at the U.S. income percentiles, so the population shares are the U.S. ones and each French group can stand in for its U.S. counterpart in the counterfactuals of section OA.3.4. The productivity profile is flatter than the U.S. one and the propensity to vote is nearly flat.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the taste for leisure differs across the groups, identified from relative hours, and rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart than under the common \(X\); the population shares and the propensities to vote are data and do not change.

Table 8 of the paper: the UK’s households at its own cuts, half-mean and mean income as for the U.S., which put most of them in the medium group. The propensity to vote rises with income, less steeply than in the U.S.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the taste for leisure differs across the groups, identified from relative hours, and rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart than under the common \(X\); the population shares and the propensities to vote are data and do not change.

Table 9 of the paper: France’s households regrouped at the UK’s income percentiles, the groups imposed on the UK in section OA.3.5 and, with the design chosen, in section OA.4.3. Propensities to vote are observed at the U.S. cuts only, so each group carries the population-weighted average of the observed values it overlaps. At these cuts France’s productivity spread is wider than the UK’s (table 8 of the paper).

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the taste for leisure differs across the groups, identified from relative hours, and rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart than under the common \(X\); the population shares and the propensities to vote are data and do not change. At these cuts France’s productivity spread is narrower than the UK’s (table OA.15), where under the common \(X\) it is wider.

The UK’s households regrouped at the U.S. income percentiles, so the population shares are the U.S. ones. At these cuts the UK’s productivity profile is much flatter than at its own (table 8 of the paper), the source of the low dispersion of relative incomes in the regrouped row of table 4 of the paper.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the taste for leisure differs across the groups, identified from relative hours, and rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart than under the common \(X\); the population shares and the propensities to vote are data and do not change.

OA.3.2 The vector-\(X_i\) calibration

The paper identifies each income group’s productivity and taste for leisure by taking the taste for leisure common across groups and fixing its level by the average workweek, so that relative hours are a prediction. The alternative takes the observed relative hours as data as well, which identifies one \(X_i\) per group and leaves the level of hours unidentified. The productivity distribution reaches every aggregate only through \(\sum_i \gamma_i \eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}\), which both calibrations normalize to one, so the calibration is block recursive: what depends on the design or on the demography is the same under both, exactly in the log case and, in the CRRA solves for the UK and France, to within one unit of the last printed digit, and only what is defined through \(\eta_i\) or \(X_i\) separately can move. The table compares every exhibit that exists under both calibrations, cell by cell, the Argentine exhibits of OA.2 included; on each exhibit, the calibration switch and mark the cells that differ show the same comparison in place.

OA.3.3 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity

The figure and the table print the parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid, for each country. Sections 6 and 7 explain the CRRA results by how the calibration absorbs a higher IES; these are the numbers behind that explanation. Matching the U.S. targets at an IES of 0.6 or below takes a thirty-year discount factor above one, which the UK and France inherit.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

One line per country; the discount factor is the U.S. one in all three. The political weight of the old falls as the IES rises in every country, since the young resist taxation less, and keeps its ranking, highest in the U.S. and lowest in the UK; the savings rate falls in every country, and the interest factor of the UK and France, a prediction, rises toward the U.S. target.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration there is no common taste for leisure to draw, and every other panel is that of the common \(X\) up to the last printed digit.

OA.3.4 Counterfactuals on the U.S.

The paper’s overview figure of section 6 collects the effect of each counterfactual on the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek at three values of the IES. Each counterfactual is a separate equilibrium path read in 2020: one characteristic of the U.S. calibration is changed over the whole horizon and every other parameter, the political weight of the old included, stays at its U.S. value, so a row describes an economy that has always had that characteristic. The tables print the effects: the pension design and ageing at the paper’s benchmark, with the economic-equilibrium effect, in which the tax rate is held at its baseline path, beside the full one; France’s income distribution, leisure preferences and voting patterns one at a time and all at once, next to France’s own calibrated path; and the same counterfactuals at each IES. Click a bar for its row.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

Figure 6.1 of the paper: one row per characteristic changed in the U.S. calibration, at three values of the IES. The design and ageing dominate the tax panel at an IES of one or below, while at an IES of two France’s voting patterns move the tax rate by more than the whole range of the design. France’s leisure preferences dominate the workweek panel and leave the tax and savings rates essentially unchanged.

Only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ from the paper’s figure: France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and lengthens the workweek by more at every IES, and its leisure preferences shorten the workweek a little less. The rows for the design, ageing and voting patterns are the paper’s.

The design at its two corners against the observed one, at an IES of one. Moving to flat benefits raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek; with the tax held at its baseline path it raises the savings rate instead, so the tax response is what lowers it, while for hours the two effects point the same way. Fully earnings-related benefits reverse every sign.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

The two ageing scenarios at an IES of one. Ageing raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek, acute ageing by more than mild; with the tax held at its baseline path the savings rate does not move and the workweek lengthens, so both falls come from the tax response.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

France’s characteristics on the U.S. at an IES of one. France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate and the workweek, its voting patterns raise the tax rate, and its leisure preferences shorten the workweek and move nothing else. All three together bring the workweek close to France’s but move the tax rate away from it.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ: France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate by more, alone and with the other characteristics, and the workweek is longer in each of these rows. Every sign is that of the common \(X\), and the voting row and France’s own path are unchanged.

The design at its two corners at each IES. Flat benefits raise the tax rate and shorten the workweek at every IES and fully earnings-related ones do the reverse, both by less the higher the IES, since the calibration then needs a lower political weight of the old and the difference between rich and poor retirees counts for less. Flat benefits lower the savings rate at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 but raise it a little at \(\rho = 2\), where both corners raise it.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

The two ageing scenarios at each IES. Ageing raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek at every IES, acute ageing by more than mild, and the tax response falls only a little as the IES rises, where that of the design falls steeply (table OA.27).

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

France’s characteristics on the U.S. at each IES. The income distribution lowers the tax rate at every IES and the voting patterns raise it, the first by less and the second by more the higher the IES, and the leisure preferences move essentially the workweek alone. With all three together the tax rate falls at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 and rises at \(\rho = 2\), where the voting patterns prevail.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ: the income distribution lowers the tax rate by more at every IES, and with all three characteristics together the tax rate falls at every IES, only marginally at \(\rho = 2\), where under the common \(X\) it rises. The voting rows are those of the common \(X\).

OA.3.5 The UK as host

The counterfactuals of section 6 on the UK’s own calibration, each a separate equilibrium path with one characteristic changed over the whole horizon and every other parameter at the UK’s value: France’s characteristics, with France’s households regrouped at the UK’s income percentiles, and the pension design and ageing at each IES. The figure sets the two hosts side by side for France’s characteristics; the tables print the UK’s numbers. Two differences from the U.S. stand out. France’s income distribution raises the UK’s tax rate where it lowers the U.S. one, because at the UK’s income cuts France is the more unequal of the two countries (OA.3.1) and equilibrium taxes rise with inequality; and France’s taste for leisure lengthens the UK’s workweek where it shortens the U.S. one, since France’s average taste for leisure lies between the two hosts’. France’s voting profile raises the tax rate on both hosts, by more at a higher IES. The income-distribution row is also the one that depends on the calibration of the taste for leisure: under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration it lowers the UK’s tax rate, because that calibration reads part of the observed income dispersion off relative hours, which are much flatter in the UK than in France.

\(\cdot\)

Calibration

France’s characteristics on the two hosts, the U.S. in the upper row of panels and the UK in the lower, on shared axes so that the hosts compare by position; the last row imposes all three at once. Together they raise the UK’s tax rate at every IES, while on the U.S. they lower it at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 and raise it at \(\rho = 2\).

The same comparison under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration, which changes the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure. France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate on both hosts at every IES, and all three characteristics together lower it on both at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1, while at \(\rho = 2\) they raise the UK’s a little and leave the U.S. one essentially unchanged.

France’s characteristics on the UK at an IES of one, laid out as the U.S. table OA.25. France’s income distribution and voting patterns each move the UK’s tax rate by less than the U.S. one, and with all three characteristics together the UK’s tax rate rises toward France’s, where the U.S. one moves away from it.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ: France’s income distribution lowers the UK’s tax rate and raises its savings rate and workweek, the reverse of every common-\(X\) sign, and with all three characteristics together the UK’s tax rate falls a little. The voting row and France’s own path are unchanged.

France’s characteristics on the UK at each IES. Each moves the UK’s savings rate by little and the leisure preferences move the workweek alone; the income distribution and the voting patterns both raise the tax rate, by more the higher the IES, and so do all three together.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration France’s income distribution lowers the UK’s tax rate at every IES, by less the higher the IES, and all three characteristics together lower it at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 and raise it at \(\rho = 2\); the voting rows are essentially those of the common \(X\).

The design at its two corners on the UK at each IES. As on the U.S. (table OA.27), flat benefits raise the tax rate and shorten the workweek at every IES and fully earnings-related ones do the reverse, both by less the higher the IES; unlike on the U.S., flat benefits lower the savings rate at every IES.

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table differs from the common-\(X\) one only in the last printed digit of a few cells at the lowest IES, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

The two ageing scenarios on the UK at each IES. As on the U.S., ageing raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek at every IES, acute ageing by more than mild, and the tax response falls only a little as the IES rises; every effect is smaller than on the U.S. (table OA.29).

Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table differs from the common-\(X\) one only in the last printed digit of a few cells at the lowest IES, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.

Income distribution replaces \(\eta_i\) with France’s while holding \(X_i\) and \(\theta\) at their UK values, so it is a change in inequality alone. Leisure preferences keeps the UK \(\eta_i\) and rescales every \(X_i\) to France’s population-weighted mean \(X\), scaled as France’s \(\eta_i\) are in the income row; it is a pure rescaling of the hours unit and moves hours and nothing else. All French characteristics imposes France’s \(\eta_i\), level of \(X_i\) and voting weights \(\mu_i\) at once. The last row is France’s own calibrated path, its savings rate reported as the distance from the UK baseline. France’s income groups are cut at the UK’s own income percentiles here (table 9 of the paper). Vector-\(X_i\) calibration: see the note to table OA.12.
